title: Notes of Ministry - 40 - March 1976

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 40 - March 1976 (2422)/Notes of Ministry - 40 - March - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I would like to encourage every one of us to commit ourselves without reserve to God’s testimony at the moment. Difficulties may stand in the way, but we are in the time when God is wanting nothing less than a giving over of our lives to Christ. We are living in times when there is so much indifference. Some are looking for alternatives, an easier path, but God has in view, dear brethren, that He shall get a full result at the end of the dispensation. That is what the Spirit says at the end of Revelation, “The Spirit and the bride say, Come” (Revelation 22: 17)—a full and practical answer in this day in which we live. If that is to be so, it involves each brother and sister in every locality committing themselves to what the Lord is doing, and He is doing something. While Christ is on high on the Father’s throne, He has control of everything down here.

My simple exercise tonight is that He should have full control of you and me. He has died to that end. Paul tells us that He has died and lives again to that end, “that he might rule over both dead and living”, Romans 14: 9. You and I are living—“We, the living who remain”, 1 Thessalonians 4: 17. What mercy there is in that, and that we are here together amongst a company of brethren who, I think I can thankfully say, want the truth and

nothing but the truth. There is perhaps a need to be a little more magnanimous in our attitude toward one another, maybe giving more credit to where the brethren are in their souls. I love to think that the saints have a desire to go on with the truth and to make everything of Christ. That is one thing that has come to light in recent times, both in our comings together and in the ministry, that brethren seem to want to learn more of Christ. Is not that a wonderful thing? What else is there anyhow, except it be His wonderful counterpart, the assembly? Yes, the assembly remains. We are not making any assumption here today that we are it, but the assembly remains. I thank God for those who wish to continue in the truth of the recovery, in the unity of the body of Christ, and my simple exercise is that we might all commit ourselves freshly to it.

Now we older brethren have a great responsibility in this regard, that is why I read concerning Naomi and Ruth. There was never, you might have said, a more inappropriate time for a person to commit herself to the fellowship than that. There was Naomi, bereaved of her husband and two sons, and marked by bitterness. What bitterness has marked the present course of things amongst brethren, what sorrows have entered into their families! There was nothing outwardly attractive about this woman, Naomi, to cause Ruth to follow her, but she loved God’s people and knew that something had happened among them. And something has happened in our day. Let us not set it aside. Something has happened, beginning with Mr. Darby, and it is going right through. We do not boastfully say these things, but it is so, it is a movement of recovery. There is bread available in Bethlehem and Naomi says, ‘The only thing I can do is to go back there’.

She moves, and as she moves this young person Ruth is attracted by her and makes a full committal. This young woman—may it be true of a brother or a sister present here today!— commits herself to what the Lord was doing in the testimony at that moment, and she is divinely blessed. There is nothing else, dear brethren, for any of us, once we commit ourselves to the path of God’s testimony on earth at the moment, but that we shall be divinely blessed. I am absolutely assured of it. They came in in the time of the barley harvest—Christ risen. What a wonderful thing that is! Has anything prevented that truth from being a joyful matter in our souls? As we often sing, ‘Christ is risen! Hallelujah!’. What can alter that? Nothing! Christ is risen; that is what Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15: 20. He is the first-fruits, and soon, dear brethren, all His own, including those that are in the grave, will hear that wonderful assembling shout and we shall all be caught up to meet the Lord in the air. But what a moment it is now to be committed to God’s testimony.

So the language of Ruth comes freshly to me, “Do not intreat me to leave thee, to return from following after thee; for whither thou goest I will go ... thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God; where thou diest will I die, and there will I be buried”. This is the language of an exercised soul in the day in which we live, wanting nothing but to commit herself to what Naomi represents—a return. How many of us need to return! We need to return to first principles. What we go on with is not sectarian—not a bit of it! If we are going on with anything it is, as Mr. Taylor said, a return to first principles. We are not setting up anything new, and we are not looking for anything new. We are not looking for alternatives. Many are, and I hope there is not one present today looking

for alternatives. What God did 150 years ago in Mr. Darby’s time was a sovereign movement of God Himself—“Then the Lord awoke”, we read in Psalm 78: 65; He did certain things and from that day onwards it has been a movement forward. There have been many divisions, many have gone back, even in recent times, but the Lord says, “Will ye also go away?”, John 6: 67. What a word that is to us today, lest there should be someone here thinking that it is not worth going on with. I can assure you the path of the righteous is worth going on with. It goes on and brightens until the day be fully come (Proverbs 4: 18).

So this dear woman, Ruth, commits herself in what outwardly was a most inappropriate time, and that is the present position. Let me assure you the Lord’s eye is upon us as to what decisions we are making in this time of difficulty. Remember what Elijah said, “How long do ye halt between two opinions?”, 1 Kings 18: 21. Is that the condition of soul of anyone here present today? There is to be only one opinion, and only one decision can rightly be made today, and that is to commit ourselves to Christ as Lord and to commit ourselves to the testimony down here as we know it in the time of recovery, in spite of all the difficulties. That is what this dear woman did and she comes in for the best. She comes in for a link with Boaz, the mighty man of wealth. Oh what a mighty Man of wealth Christ is! “The Father loves the Son, and has given all things to be in his hand”, John 3: 35. The whole administration now is not a legal one, it is in the hands of the Son; He is Son over God’s house. How much He is ready to dispense to us! The more dependent we are, the more diligent we are, the more we go on with our secret histories with God, the more we shall prove how much the Son has to dispense in every locality.

Oh may we be freshly stirred, dear brethren, to go on to some sense of finality in our soul exercises and come through to what Ruth reached in type, union with Christ. That is what we are looking forward to on the morrow, something for Christ. Our side has been met. All our liabilities have been met by the blood of Jesus. We have the eternal prospect before us of being with Him where He is. He has died to deliver us from this present evil world and to give us a present part and place amongst His so great a people. Then, finally, we have the prospect of being with Him. He is soon coming. That is the word that the Lord says to some of those assemblies in the Revelation. He does not tell them to try to make things better down here. I know there is such a thing as making our local conditions better, but you cannot set up something now like Pentecost. But the Lord says, “I come quickly—hold fast what thou hast”, Revelation 3: 11. Let us do it; let us hold fast to the treasure we have. It has been secured at much cost and suffering. Men of God have laid themselves out for a secret history with God and they have brought to us a heritage of ministry, of truth, that is a great stand-by in the day in which we live, though we cannot exactly live on it. Do not misunderstand me, but you cannot live on the bookshelf. If you are going to live at all you live by Christ; “He also who eats me shall live also on account of me”, John 6: 57. The previous verse shows that we are to eat His flesh and drink His blood also. No, you cannot live on the bookshelf. I may quote a good many things here today, but I want my heart filled with Christ. It is He that causes us to make a decision for Him and for His people, and that is what Ruth did—“Thy people shall be my people”.

You may say, They are a poor lot, making all these mistakes, doing this and that, but you could not deter Ruth. It is the work of God coming out in her, and that is what we want, the work of God coming out and asserting itself in devotion and committal to Christ. The Lord is looking for it today, dear brethren.

It was the same with Ittai. When was it outwardly a more inappropriate time than in the days of Ittai to commit oneself to a rejected David? Was it a prosperous time? It certainly was not. David was on the run. It was a suffering time for David and it is a suffering time for the testimony now. Paul tells Timothy, “Take thy share in suffering as a good soldier of Jesus Christ”, 2 Timothy 2: 3. But he also says, “Remember Jesus Christ raised from among the dead, of the seed of David” (verse 8). These words of Paul are calculated, I think, to stir us up in our hearts as to the salient features of the truth connected with christianity itself, the death of Christ, the resurrection of Christ, the ascension of Christ, and the Spirit down here. What a wonderful thing that the Spirit is here, dear brethren. Are we at a loss? Not a bit of it! Small numbers? Two or three brothers and sisters in a place, sometimes one brother—Are we at a loss? No! If the Lord has put His hand upon a place to put something of assembly character there, He has committed Himself to it. We are never at a loss with the Lord and the Spirit with us. All that is called for, dear brethren, on our side is this secret history and committal, such as you get here with Ittai.
He is tested. David said in effect, ‘What are you doing following me? I am going where I can. It is a time of suffering’. Here we are today, and what suffering there is. You look

around upon the dear brethren and see them suffering family-wise and circumstantially. Does it deter an Ittai? He is a Philistine, you know, from Gath. He is a converted Philistine. There is certainly room for converted Philistines in these days, dear brethren. There is a danger with some of us of developing things in the head. But this man is not like that, he is a converted man, and he is an influential man. What is called for, I think, in all our localities in these days is persons who will commit themselves and thus become influential, as were Naomi and Ittai. Ittai has six hundred men with him and little ones. He affects them all by his committal.

The best way to help the dear young people to commit themselves to the testimony is to let them see committal in us. We talk enough about these things, but let them see it. A father and mother throughout the day have their daily tasks to do, but their spare time, what are they doing with it? Are they diligently pursuing the truth? Are they on their knees before God that He may do something additionally in the locality? Such was Ittai—“In what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be”.

What we get in Philippians 3 is Paul’s inward energy of devotion for Christ. O, dear brethren, I would like to appeal to us all, myself included, to give ourselves more unreservedly, as Paul did here, his inwards, his whole being, given over to Christ. It is not a question of whether it is the time for it, or whether there is suffering or whether there are difficulties. Paul is saying in this chapter it is always time to have Christ before you as your Object. Let me add a word here, if I may. We often say that Christ is to be our

Object. The only way to prove deliverance is to have Him thus. There is such a thing as having Christ as our satisfying Object. It is easy to tell a person who is satisfied, and the only way to be satisfied is to have Christ supremely before our souls and to be pressing on. This is no time for sitting back, what is called for is inward energy in going on with the truth. This reminds us of the offerings of old. You will remember how the inwards were to be put on the altar. No doubt it applies uniquely to Christ Himself. What an offering that was as He gave Himself over, you might say, in suffering on the cross, involving His whole being (I would touch it with reverence), His inwards, what was intrinsic in Him.

Paul in this chapter would encourage us all to give ourselves over as he says, “Brethren, I do not count to have got possession myself; but one thing—forgetting the things behind, and stretching out to the things before, I pursue”. Stretching out is an athletic reference, showing that the matter is urgent. There is something before us. What else can be rightly before us in these days but Christ in His own intrinsic, essential worth and what belongs to Him down here in His assembly? He says, “My assembly”. Let us learn, dear brethren, as we beseech one another today, to give ourselves over to secret history with God, so that the assembly locally and universally may be prospered from this day forward. Let us keep our hearts and our eyes firmly upon Christ and what is precious to Him down here, as those who care for the things of Jesus Christ. Paul says, “All seek their own things, not the things of Jesus Christ”, Philippians 2: 21. .This is a time, dear brethren, to seek the things of Jesus Christ, things that really matter, things that really last, things that call down divine approval. May it be the portion of
us all, for His name’s sake.

I would like to say a word, dear brethren, as the Lord may help, as to the relationship which develops in this book between Mordecai and Esther. The book itself is an interesting one, finding its place in the holy writings, and yet, as we have often been reminded, the name of God is not mentioned in it, and prayer is not mentioned in it. But there are certain features developed which, under the hand of the Spirit of God, are intended to impress us with the qualities that are to mark the saints in a day of darkness, a day when God is not acknowledging formally His relationship with His people, when there is no public intervention on their behalf, but when heaven’s initiative is very clearly to be seen in making room for the qualities which heaven approves and which heaven vindicates.

The background is one of dislocated relations. The rejection of Vashti, who did not acknowledge the claim of king Ahasuerus, reminds us of what is only too prevalent around, where the creatorial relationship between the man and the woman is largely becoming disregarded, something about which we do well to be alerted. I do not dwell on that, save to emphasize that God has set man

in man’s place and woman in woman’s place. Vashti got out of her place and she is removed from being queen. This makes way, in the skill of the Spirit of God, for the bringing into view of another in Esther. It has often been said that we have in this book the removal of the first and the establishment of the second in relation to the assembly. I believe that we should be alert to the emergence among us in the testimony of assembly qualities. We have been considering earlier the servant taking that long journey to secure a bride for Isaac. He was by the well, alert, speaking in his heart, his affections active in relation to the features that would come to light which were fully in keeping with the mind of heaven.

Mordecai really represents the spirit of Christ. I believe we need a Mordecai in every one of our localities. Esther became queen, she became influential in the whole realm, but the first person to appreciate Esther’s qualities was Mordecai. Dear brother or sister, there is need that you should watch in your locality for the emergence of subjective features that are proper to the assembly. Esther, it says, “had neither father nor mother”; she is cut off from natural resource, and thus Mordecai accepts responsibility for her. What a touch that is! We need to accept responsibility for the virgin qualities proper to the work of God which may be coming to light in our localities. Thank God for the number of young persons here today. Watch over them! Look for what may show itself in the way of virgin affection for Christ, and see that that is nourished, see that it is developed, see, that it is protected. It says, “Mordecai took her for his own daughter”. He was committing himself, you might say, to see that this feature, so precious under his discerning eye, should not be damaged but should be preserved
for whatever purpose God might intend in the testimony.

Satan is very active to damage persons so that they should not be available in God’s testimony. He would attempt through one means and another to divert your attention by what is earthly, by what is worldly, by what comes from beneath instead of what comes from above. He would spoil you, giving you a taste for what is adverse, instead of your being preserved in an environment where you can be used and where you can develop normally in relation to the things of God. What we should look for is normal growth. It says, “Mordecai walked every day before the court … to know how Esther did”, Esther 2: 11. That is, he committed himself; he felt responsible for her, and he was very concerned as to what was developing in her.

So the time comes when she is to go in to the king. It says, “when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter, came to go in to the king, she required nothing but what Hegai the king’s chamberlain, keeper of the women, appointed”. I think the link between the Spirit in type and this assembly quality is most instructive. We have spoken of Rebecca, herself a personality. Esther became a personality in her own right and she required nothing additional. She was entirely in subjection to what was provided for her, in figure, by the Spirit. Another has said that dependence is a feature of moral kindredship with Christ, and I am sure that is true. She was entirely dependent on what was provided for her by the Spirit. Hegai is a type of the Spirit of God, linking on with Mordecai and furnishing all that was needed, so that when the time came Esther was accepted; “she obtained grace in the

sight of all them that saw her”. It is wonderful when you see features which have been nourished, treasured, and nurtured according to God develop and become wider in their influence as God makes room for them in His ways in the testimony.

Esther 3 brings out another important point. The king promotes “Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite”. We should be aware, dear brethren, that the enemy is always against what is giving pleasure to heaven. If something has been developing and has come to maturity and is now accepting responsibility in relation to the testimony. Satan is against that. His attack is incessant. He does not give up, but comes back again and again. So the king promotes Haman and the consequence is that men are to bow to him. “All the king’s servants that were in the king’s gate bowed and did Haman reverence”. A principle is introduced to which persons are expected to bow. Then it says, “Mordecai bowed not”.

I am going to appeal, dear brethren, for moral integrity in those who accept responsibility in our localities. A principle is brought in, an Amalekitish principle, and “Mordecai bowed not”. Why do you think that was? The history of the Amalekite in Scripture goes right back to Rephidim. The Amalekite was against the testimony of God. He is not a foe dealt with just once, it is a recurring conflict. The Amalekite attack happens over and over again, as with the Philistines who represent another principle which seems to assert itself time and time again, asserting themselves in the book of Judges, utterly defeated under Samson, yet when you come to David’s day they are spreading themselves over the land (2 Samuel 5: 18, 22). So Satan is unrelenting, but he has certain known lines of attack. This is one of them, the Amalekite.

He is not only against the testimony, but he is against God. We learn in Exodus that his hand is on the throne of Jah (Exodus 17: 16), showing how Satan would challenge the supremacy of God in relation to what is precious to Him.

So it says that “Mordecai bowed not”. O, dear brethren, can I appeal for faithfulness, for a knowledge of what has gone before in the testimony, and for strength and courage to resist what would overthrow what is precious to Christ. Saul was instructed to deal with the Amalekite but it says he spared the best (1 Samuel 15: 9). He was selective, he did not carry the thing through to its right conclusion according to God. Jehovah having “war with Amalek from generation to generation”, Exodus 17: 16. So Agag comes to Samuel and says, “Surely the bitterness of death is past”, 1 Samuel 15: 32. He came gaily. Amalek will put on a big display; man in the flesh is always able to do that. But it says, “Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before Jehovah”. Oh let us be true, dear brethren, in our localities to conflicts that have been fought and won. The enemy is always asserting himself, but the Spirit of Christ is here seen in Mordecai; it says he “bowed not”. Thank God for what is amongst us that is not prepared to bow to an Amalekite principle.

This results in the testimony being brought into suffering. Mordecai in the beginning of Esther 4 “put on sackcloth with ashes and went out into the midst of the city, and cried with a loud and bitter cry”. The reproach of Christ is to be accepted. If we are to be true to these beautiful assembly features, if they are to be protected, if they are to be preserved, if they are to become influential as God intends they should be, we need to accept the position of

reproach. Mordecai gives a lead. The principle of leadership was never more needed amongst us. It has been abused; we have spoken of it in a way which was unwise, and Satan has exploited it; but the principle of leadership remains—not the sort of leadership that would assert its own right over the saints, but the leadership that in devotion to Christ simply goes before, goes before in the acceptance of the obligations, the burdens, the sufferings, of the testimony. This is the kind of leadership that God will support, and it is seen in Mordecai. He kept himself first—he did not bow to the Amalekite, and then he is used. His moral influence extends to the whole area that is around him as he accepts the position of suffering.

Esther is not at first equal to this. We need to be patient with one another, dear brethren. All may not see the issue as clearly as you do; all may not be ready at the first onset to commit themselves fully to the position of suffering. Mordecai goes on and Esther is brought round. She seeks to soften the position, even as Peter, drawing alongside the Lord said, “This shall in no wise be unto thee” (Matthew 16: 22), seeking to soften the severity of the suffering into which the Lord Himself was moving. So Esther would seek to modify, to remove the sackcloth, to say, ‘Well, there is no need for a position of public reproach’. Do you remember that as the children of Israel went out of Egypt it says they “went out ... in the sight of all the Egyptians”, Numbers 33: 3. It was a public matter; it was not a secret matter; it was seen that they had gone out. Mr. Taylor said that if we are not publicly out of the world, we are not out of it rightly (N.S. Vol. 13, p.169). We are to be committed to a position of reproach.
So Mordecai remains true and Esther is brought

round, until at the end of Esther 4 her language is beautiful. Mordecai having spoken to her and exhorted her, she says, “Go, gather together all the Jews that are found in Shushan, and fast for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day—I also and my maidens will fast likewise, and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law; and if I perish, I perish”. What a committal! What language! This feature of the assembly is now seen not simply as able to answer to the affections of the king, but as equal to the acceptance of her place sufferingly in the testimony of God. Oh that these things should be more worked out in our localities! “If I perish, I perish”—an irrevocable committal. She is out and out, she is committing herself fully now to the testimony of God. The influence of Mordecai is such that she is now completely devoted to what God is doing, prepared, as was Moses of old, “rather to suffer affliction along with the people of God than to have the temporary pleasure of sin”, Hebrews 11: 25. God will answer this. He answers committal to His rights. Mordecai stood for them—Esther comes under his influence and God answers it, so that the position is turned in her favour and the king holds out to Esther the golden sceptre. God is acting, you see. I think we should have the assurance that in spite of God not being mentioned in this book the initiative of heaven was never more realised by those that are true.

So the golden sceptre is held out to Esther and the word is, “What wilt thou, queen Esther?” (Esther 5: 3). Notice, “queen Esther”, a royal touch. The name Esther means a star and connects with what we have been saying today as to personality that is heavenly. She is now in a position where she can dictate her own terms; she has the initiative. What was against the people of God

had seemed to have the initiative but now, through this beautiful committal, the initiative has passed; Esther has it and the question is, “What wilt thou?”. It is a wonderful day when we realise in our localities that the assembly has the initiative. God would see that it is so—not simply a particular person, not simply leadership, right in its place, but that the assembly has the initiative. Esther is going to use it now. Certain things are active against the testimony of God. Having a clear judgment of them she is now going to use the initiative that God has given her.

One feature of the assembly is the exercise of wisdom in matters of administration, a feature much needed. So Esther waits for two days. She calls a feast on the first day and then she calls another feast on another day. The initiative is held; power is there. You might say that executive action could have been taken on the first day, but Esther waits. What instances there are in Scripture of the wisdom in waiting. In the rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram Moses says, “Be thou and all thy band before Jehovah ... tomorrow” and again, “Even tomorrow will Jehovah make known who is his”, Numbers 16: 16, 5. This shows the ability to wait. Let us not be hasty, dear brethren, let us rather represent heaven in what we do, aware that the initiative is in the assembly and can be trusted there.

The waiting time historically according to this record results in Mordecai’s influence being extended as “the man whom the king delights to honour”. The waiting time is turned to advantage, so that when the moment comes everything is in Esther’s favour. Haman, the Jew’s enemy, the great representative of Satan as against the testimony of God, is exposed fully and the matter is completely dealt with.

I would appeal then for the development of these assembly qualities, on the one hand what will answer to the affections of the Man; qualities also that will commit themselves fully in relation to the sufferings of the testimony. And then the wisdom that can wait, knowing what it is to make room for God in matters and which, although having a clear judgment of what needs to be dealt with, can defer until the right moment arrives and the position is absolutely clear. These things are very testing, they are very real, and I believe the Lord would help us to see how they apply to situations which may arise in our localities.

I read the beginning of Esther 8 because all this time the link between Mordecai and Esther had been secret. It was there in a very real sense, treasured, used by Mordecai to influence the queen, but secret. Now in chapter 8 it says, “Mordecai came before the king; for Esther had told what he was to her”. Oh what a touch, dear brethren! We think of Esther as representing the assembly, and Mordecai as representing the spirit of Christ. Esther had told what Mordecai was to her. What Christ is to the assembly is now coming fully into view. What will come into view at the end is what the assembly is to Christ. The word to Philadelphia is, they “shall know that I have loved thee”, Revelation 3: 9. What stimulation it gives to us, for a day is soon to come when they shall know. We know it now, but they shall know that “I have loved thee”. Let this be answered in a fresh committal on our side. He is true to us; let us be true to Him. Let us make it known what Mordecai is to us, what Christ is to the assembly.
I commend these things to us, dear brethren, to our interest, to our consciences, and our hearts, for God wants to get not only your mind, but your

vitals, and He wants you to be committed to these things, in the place which He has given to you in the testimony—a place to be valued, a place to be treasured, a place to be protected above all else in a day of such darkness.

articles.title: LISTENING TO PAUL
articles.author: C. S. Elliott
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.text: Acts 27: 5–This is a rather long passage, but I thought reading it would help to give the background to the whole scene that we have before us. The brethren know the passage well, but what impresses me is the thought of what could have been averted if they had listened to Paul. I believe that at the present time we shall prove it increasingly safe for our souls if we pay attention to the apostle’s word, because he had the mind of God. Here, in this setting, his word was rejected by the sailors, who probably had a great deal of experience on the seas. They may have thought, ‘Where would Paul have gained his experience to be able to speak as he does? What does he know about the sea? He is just a tentmaker; what can he know about navigation?’. But the important thing was that he had the mind of God, and that is what is needed in every situation. Do we have the mind of God? Will what we do bring glory to God? Paul had warned them earlier. He had said, “I perceive that the navigation will be with disaster and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives”.

Would we want to turn away from Paul to go by our own thoughts and to carry on as we please? It would only lead to disaster, as the men on this ship found out. The apostle Paul was with God and had the mind of God, so he brought in the word of God at the right moment. The details in the passage, if we look into them carefully, provide a wealth of knowledge, experience, and food for our souls. Those persons had to go the way they did, through distress and calamity, because they did not hearken to Paul. “The storm”, it says, was “extremely violent on us”, and then they threw the cargo overboard and cast away the ship’s furniture. Then neither sun nor stars appeared for many days. It was a dark, difficult and dismal situation. I believe that, if we turn away from Paul, that is exactly the situation in which we shall find ourselves, tossed and thrown about in every direction. How precious are the apostle’s words which he wrote to Timothy, “Let every one who names the name of the Lord withdraw from iniquity”, 2 Timothy 2: 19. How very testing that is! It comes very close; it is very penetrating, but as standing by the apostle’s word we find we are safe. The apostle is with God, so if we are with Paul then we find that God will be with us.

Here they had to go the whole way to disaster. What experiences they had! But later Paul said, “And now I exhort you to be of good courage, for there shall be no loss at all of life of any of you, only the ship. For an angel of the God, whose I am and whom I serve, stood by me this night, saying, Fear not, Paul; thou must stand before Caesar; and behold, God has granted to thee all those that sail with thee”. The apostle was now in command of the situation; he was with God. He could lay claim to God as he spoke—“The God, whose I am and whom I serve”. How he

valued the sense of grace in his soul, that he belonged to God; that God had taken him up. And we in our measure would know something of this, that God in His grace has taken us up and brought us into a sphere of blessing. But then He intends us to remain there so that we may be saved practically.

Just previously Paul had said, “Ye ought, O men, to have hearkened to me”. The word of rebuke comes home to us forcibly when we move away from the path of what is right, the path on which the Lord has set us, and in which the apostles and other men of God have walked—the path of the just. Think of what it means if we turn away from that! The word of rebuke comes sometimes, but then it might not come. It is very solemn to think that it might not come. We know that for many the word of rebuke has come but has not been heeded and such have lost their way. But if the rebuke comes, and we heed it, and are brought back to what is right, let us give glory to God.

Later, Paul says, “I exhort you to partake of food, for this has to do with your safety; for not a hair from the head of any one of you shall perish”. If we have someone like that on board, what an exhortation, what a comfort! Paul brings in the mind of God—and how much needed that is. I cannot over-emphasise the need of bringing in the mind of God so that souls are saved. Then, later on, it says, “The counsel of the soldiers was that they should kill the prisoners, lest any one should swim off and escape”. There seems to be no gratitude to Paul on the part of the soldiers for saving their lives. There was this man of God on board, but they were more concerned lest any one might swim

off and escape. We do not want to be like that; we want to be on the line of saving souls, of preserving persons alive. Then some cast themselves into the sea to get to land, while the rest, some on boards, others on some of the things that came from the ship, all got safe to land. As way was made for Paul, they all got safe to land. We want to prove that, getting to land, and the saints being preserved; what is for God preserved among His people, so that there can be glory to God.

I have been impressed as to what comes through death, in type, and I believe that would apply here. Think of the waters through which they passed, but they came through safely to land. May right conditions be maintained by us; may we be listening to Paul, obedient to his word, and thus be preserved for the glory of God.

“HAVING LAID HIS HANDS ON EVERY ONE OF THEM”—Mark 4: 40 records the affecting scene when, the sun having gone down, as many as had persons sick brought them to Jesus. It says, “Having laid his hands on every one of them, he healed them”. It was not a momentary touch, but a lingering handling of each one, conveying a divine wealth of love, compassion, and healing power. If, through grace, we have had such an experience with the Lord Jesus let us give thanks for it and rejoice in it. But when He laid His hands on you and on me it was not only to impart the assurance of forgiveness and healing, but to claim us unreservedly for Himself.

Have we yielded to His longing, and His right, to have us for His own pleasure and service? He died, Paul says, “That they who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who died for them and has been raised”, 2 Corinthians 5: 15. May we have a deepening consciousness of what the laying on of His hands means and, as yielding to it, be in the happy path of subjection to His will. Mark also tells us of the colt tied, and the word as to it was, “The Lord has need of it”, Mark 11: 3. He has drawn near to us not only because we needed Him, but because He needed us—amazing fact! He needs you for the most privileged part you could possibly have, the greatest dignity that could be conferred upon you—that your life and your all should be devoted to Him. He has a place for you, and the Holy Spirit is available to show you what it is and to enable you to fill it.

Now I would urge prayer. How much do we pray, dear brethren? How far do we travel in our prayers? The more you are with God the wider shall become the area covered by your prayers, until the whole household of faith is embraced, and indeed ‘all men’. Do not be satisfied with your prayers until you, as it were, cover the whole household of faith … It is a wonderful experience to have to say to God, and as you pray and embrace the saints in your prayers, you get an impression from God; you become assured He has heard you.

If we had truly died with Christ we should be morally severed from everything here; yet we should carry out every duty better than ever, because we should be solely dependent on Christ. No one can understand eternal life until he is in it, I mean, until he is enjoying it. With most christians what is sought is not to live with Christ where He is, but to obtain His help where we are. Both are ours, but while the greater leads to the lesser, the lesser does not include the greater.
paragraphs.source: J. B. Stoney (‘Letters’, 2nd Series, Vol. III, p.272)

paragraphs.text: Then he (Paul) proceeds to show how things were worked out in himself, which is another great thing. One might say to Paul—You have been telling us a good deal, giving nice addresses, and have stood on doctrinal lines ... but how have things been worked out in your own soul? That is how, as in service, we should challenge ourselves ... I do not know anything more effective in a way, than that a preacher can tell how the truth has come about in his own soul. That is what Paul is able to do above all others; he is able to tell us in Romans how things were worked out in his own soul.
A spiritual man is one who makes full room for the Spirit in himself.
